articles.title_orig: Spain snap election: PM Sanchez calls November election amid growing housing protests
articles.title_zh: Spain snap election: PM Sanchez calls November election amid growing housing protests
articles.content_orig:
Spanish Prime ⁠Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called ⁠an ​early ​election in an apparent effort to seize the initiative following nationwide protests over a housing crisis sparked by the eviction of a 87-year-old woman.
The election, scheduled for ​November ⁠29, will bring the current parliamentary term to an end more than six months ahead of schedule.
“After informing the head of state, I have decided to convene an extraordinary meeting of the Council of Ministers this morning to dissolve Parliament and call a general election,” Sánchez, leader of the Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), said in a televised address from Moncloa, his official residence in Madrid.
The announcement came after Sánchez’s government last week failed to secure parliamentary backing for two propsoed laws aimed at tackling the country’s housing crisis.
The measures were proposed following mounting public anger at the eviction of Maria del Carmen Abascal, known in Spain simply as Maricarmen, an 87-year-old resident of Madrid’s Retiro neighborhood, whose case has become a symbol of the country’s housing emergency.
Maricarmen had been living in the same house for more than 70 years but was evicted after her rent increased from €500 ($560) to €2,650 ($2,970). Thousands of people took to the streets in fury, and she has become the face of the ruthlessness of Spain’s housing crisis.
For more than a week, hundreds of people have camped out in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol to protest the crisis, and rallies have taken place elsewhere in Spain.
Madrid’s Tenants Union, one of the groups organizing the protests, claimed about 950,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country over the weekend.
Sánchez, who has been prime minister for more than eight years, called the election three days after right-wing parties in parliament defeated proposed laws aimed to ease the hosuing crisis.
Analysts expect Sánchez to focus on housing in an effort to win over popular support. The conservative Popular Party, which opposed the ptoposed housing reforms, is leading in opinion polls.
“We need to renew people’s support,” Sánchez said on Monday. “We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.”
Sánchez’s socialist PSOE party has suffered several setbacks in regional elections this year, and a series of corruption scandals involving close associates have also tarnished its reputation.
The migration crisis in Ceuta - in which tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the Spainish terriority bordering Morocco - during the summer intensified that criticism.
“I know that among part of that social majority there is dissatisfaction today,” he said. “You are outraged to see their interests being trampled on in Parliament for the benefit of a select few.”
As he called for snap elections, he conceded his government had made some “mistakes” but argued it had been faced with unprecedented challenges from abroad. He cited the war in Ukraine and the conflicts in the Middle East, he also highlighted Spain becoming one of Europe’s strongest economies.
Sánchez is one of the few center-left leaders in Europe amid a surge in right-wing populism, and he has taken a firm stand on issues such as Palestinian statehood, the responsibility of social media companies and the US campaign against Iran.
Spain refused to allow US bombers to use bases on its territory. Sánchez has been outspoken in his criticism of US strikes, provoking anger and threats from the White House. But rather than back down, Sánchez and his government doubled down, winning public support for his opposition to the Trump administration.
In March, Trump threatened to cut off trade with Spain. “We could use their base if we want, we could just fly in and use it, nobody’s going to tell us not to use it,” he said.
In contrast to much of Europe, Sánchez has also said that immigration is essential to sustain economic growth and moved to regularize the status of hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants in Spain earlier this year.
“I trust my fellow citizens,” Sánchez went on to say. “I know that you are a courageous and compassionate people who rise to challenges, and that you have no qualms about being the first, and the last, to stand on the right side of history.”
Sánchez has put together a series of coalitions with left-wing parties and small separatist parties over the past eight years but has struggled to get legislation through at times, often falling back on decrees. The government has been unable to pass a budget for three years.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the center-right People’s Party (PP) with the support of the far-right Vox party is the most likely outcome in the election. If Vox were to join an incoming government, it would be the first time the far-right would be part of a government in Spain since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.

articles.title_orig: France to shutter up to 500 schools as more student protests called
articles.title_zh: France to shutter up to 500 schools as more student protests called
articles.content_orig:
France plans to fully or partially close up to 500 schools on Monday amid a series of student protests that have become increasingly violent .
Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced the precautionary measures on Sunday as part of a bid for a “partial, progressive return to lessons”. However, after a weekend lull, student protestors announced they plan to resume demonstrations – launched last month over complaints regarding class sizes, lack of teachers, and other complaints – early in the week.
Lessons will be “totally or partly suspended” in some “400-500” high schools as the security conditions “have not been fulfilled”, the minister said. He added that 24 schools had been “burned or ransacked” since the start of the protests.
Geffray said the closures were a security precaution. Protest organisers have called for a return to large-scale demonstrations on Tuesday, citing a lack of “concrete measures” from President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
At least 170 students and 78 educational personnel have been injured since the student demos first erupted in the Paris region in mid-September, according to Geffray.
The Ministry of National Education reported that at least 400 of the 3,700 high schools in France were closed on Friday , while 560 faced protests or disruptions.
The number of schools affected on Monday would be comparable to the figure from Friday, Geffray said.
Teachers and students first mobilised at a high school in a Paris suburb on 17 September over a lack of teaching staff, excessive school-day hours and other grievances . The protests have since spread nationwide, resulting in class strikes, blockades and demonstrations.
According to the interior minister, more than 5,000 people have been arrested in the last week; 85 percent of them minors.
Critics have criticised “disproportionate” police violence in response to the demonstrations. Rights group Amnesty International said the student protestors “must be listened to, not repressed”.
In an interview on French public radio, Geffray claimed far-left activists “infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves and engaged in extreme violence.”

A Southern California boy faces a potentially lengthy recovery after being hospitalized with West Nile virus, prompting his mother to warn other parents about the early signs as Los Angeles County sees a record number of mosquito-borne infections.
As 13-year-old Joseph Vasquez remains unable to walk while being treated at Los Angeles Children's Hospital, his mother, Maria Salazar, told NBC Los Angeles that she was fearful her son could die.
Stream Los Angeles News for free, 24/7, wherever you are.
It all started with a rash that looked like chickenpox, according to Salazar. Then Joseph took a fall at school before developing other symptoms, including a fever, loss of appetite and headaches.
"We ended up taking him to the emergency room because I found him facedown on the ground," the mother said, explaining that Joseph had been losing his balance before he was diagnosed with West Nile virus. "It just started to be from the lower body, and then he couldn't even feel his toes or movement."
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that about 80% of West Nile virus infections are asymptomatic, while less than 1% of infected people develop neuroinvasive disease.
"Most of the cases, we have fever, maybe you just feel like funny," Dr. Ilan Shapiro of AltaMed Health Services said. "But there are cases, and that's why it's so important to talk about these viruses that can have problems, neurologically speaking, in our kids."
Shapiro, who is not Joseph's doctor, said inflammation caused by the infection may be making it challenging for the 13-year-old to walk.
"Our body is actually made of nerves and other things that actually connect our brain to our body. Sometimes that part of the connection can actually get inflamed, and that's where you can actually have this," the doctor explained.
Salazar, who initially thought her son had a common cold, now urges other parents to take proper precautions when kids go outdoors and pay attention to symptoms — the signs she initially brushed off.
"They should be looking out for any mosquito bites, dizziness, headaches, blurry vision, falling, losing balance," she said. "If your kids are telling you, 'Hey, my head hurts,' and they're scratching, take them to the doctor."
Dr. Shapiro said it's important to seek medical attention if people experience symptoms such as fever, chills, brain fog and fatigue, especially after spending time outdoors.
Los Angeles County has recorded 135 confirmed West Nile virus infections this year, including 130 hospitalizations and five deaths, according to the county Department of Public Health.

articles.title_orig: Here’s how Western Pa. school districts are preparing amid a statewide surge in measles cases
articles.title_zh: Here’s how Western Pa. school districts are preparing amid a statewide surge in measles cases
articles.content_orig:
Nine out of 10 unvaccinated individuals who come in contact with measles will get sick.
In late June, Chester County reported two cases of measles, as an outbreak in bordering Lancaster County crossed into the farmlands that blend into the suburban sprawl of Philadelphia’s collar communities.
Case numbers grew tenfold in July, and by late August, three dozen people had gotten sick up and down the county’s western border.
The latest numbers now show 83 measles cases in Chester County , more than most entire states have seen all year, making it a locus in Pennsylvania’s largest measles outbreak in more than three decades.
Chester is the first county in the Philadelphia region to grapple with wide circulation of a highly contagious virus that could spread like wildfire if it reaches other under-vaccinated communities, especially densely populated ones closer to the city.
As cases rise in Chester County, public health officials are ramping up educational outreach, scheduling pop-up clinics, and even bringing doses of the vaccine to people’s homes, all in an effort to contain known hot spots in the outbreak.
At Chester County’s schools, homecoming parades, and grocery stores, many families say they are aware of the outbreak, but are not deeply concerned. Those who are vaccinated worry more that their social and school lives may be disrupted, as they were during the COVID-19 pandemic, if the virus continues to spread.
Anne Nemeth, who lives in Paradise in Lancaster County, feels only a little worried, given that her two sons are vaccinated.
At a time of declining vaccination rates , she isn’t sure whether some of her closest neighbors, who the family regularly gets together with, are vaccinated.
They are Amish, and she has read that many of the people getting sick in her area were part of the Plain community. Two Amish infants in Lancaster County died in August after contracting measles in the state’s first deaths linked to the outbreak.
“I’m hoping they would tell us if they were sick,” she said. “It’s a lot of trust.”
Pennsylvania has reported five deaths associated with measles. A 20-year-old Amish woman who died lived just over the Chester border in Lancaster County. She wanted the vaccine after her parents and eight siblings got sick, but couldn’t get it because she was being treated for leukemia.
Close to 1,000 people statewide have been sickened by the virus, marking one of the most robust outbreaks the United States has seen in years. And experts say the cases that have been reported are likely an undercount, as many people do not seek medical care for their symptoms and some have been reluctant to speak with the health department.
“Public health is now in a race with the disease,” said Dale Weiser, the clinical services supervisor for Chester County’s health department. “It’s going to either burn through all the susceptible people, or we’re going to make fewer people susceptible through vaccination. That’s the only way it ends.”
Measles is so contagious that nine out of 10 unvaccinated individuals who come in contact with the disease will get sick.
That’s how a county like Chester, with one of the highest vaccination rates in the state, has also come to log the third-most cases in the outbreak.
Chester County’s kindergarten measles vaccination rate falls just below the 95% threshold that scientists say is necessary to keep the virus from spreading widely. Kindergarten vaccination offers a view into a community’s protection because the vaccines are required for school attendance.
But the county — like the rest of the Philadelphia region — is pockmarked with areas where vaccination has dropped well below the so-called herd immunity threshold, leaving families vulnerable to severe illness.
In eastern Chester County, for instance, five elementary schools in West Chester had kindergarten measles vaccination rates below 95% — one of the vulnerable areas in the region identified by an Inquirer analysis of 2025-26 school-level data.
Farther east, Chester City in Delaware County , and neighborhoods in West and North Philadelphia have also similarly seen measles vaccination rates drop below so-called herd immunity.
In Chester County, the health department seeks to limit the virus from spreading from west to east across the county, where it would reach more densely populated communities, said Jeanne Franklin, Chester County’s health director.
“If it finds that pocket of unvaccinated individuals, it’s going to popcorn until it finds no one left,” Franklin said.
The health department began reaching out to hospitals and schools months before Chester County reported its first cases, because public health leaders knew it was likely only a matter of time before the virus spread from Lancaster County, Franklin said.
Hospitals were asked to develop a measles screening protocol, if they didn’t have it already, so that early symptoms, such as fever, cough, and runny nose, wouldn’t be dismissed as seasonal illnesses.
Schools were urged to start tracking vaccine status among staff. When a school identifies a measles case, the county requires any student or staff member who is unvaccinated or does not have proof of vaccination to stay home for 21 days, Franklin said. Since many adults don’t have their vaccination records handy, that could create a major staffing disruption.
As case counts in Chester County grow, pop-up vaccine clinics have been scheduled across the county.
The health department has administered more than 500 doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine so far this year, most of them since the outbreak began in April.
The health department’s nurses will bring doses of the vaccine to homes and farms of residents who don’t travel. Vaccines are also available at the county’s health clinics.
Many of the parents lined up along Atglen’s Main Street last week for the local school district’s homecoming parade said they did not feel a reason to be deeply concerned about the outbreak because their families are vaccinated.
“I guess I have the same level of concern as I have for all sickness with kids in public schools,” said Sandi Wrigley, a Cochranville mother whose children, ages 9 and 11, are vaccinated. “If we take the time to worry about that, it’ll be an endless worry.”
Until recently, measles was considered eradicated in the United States, and despite declining vaccination rates, most families are still choosing to vaccinate their children.
Some were angry that measles is even a conversation.
Michael Lavender, from Parkesburg, said vaccinating his 12-year-old daughter was an “easy decision.”
“I really feel like there should be no reason to even talk about it,” he said.
On the other side of the county, families lined up inside the Great Valley Middle School gymnasium in Malvern for flu and COVID-19 vaccines.
Kevin Wrabley, of Malvern, doesn’t worry about his 11-year-old son contracting measles because he is vaccinated. But he does worry about other children and adults who aren’t able to get vaccinated.
“It’s discouraging, things we thought were safely behind us are coming back,” he said.
In Chester County, public health educators have the task of trying to untangle the myriad reasons people are opting out of a vaccination. Many have little to do with science: Two doses of the measles vaccine provide 97% protection — better than most vaccines.
The MMR vaccine is among those long required to attend school in Pennsylvania and every other state. But families here have increasingly been deciding against vaccination for religious and philosophical reasons, as state law permits, often by simply printing and signing a form noting their objection.
Some fluctuations in kindergarten vaccination rates are typical from year to year, but the rise of anti-vaccine rhetoric in federal leadership and a growing distrust in public health authorities has exacerbated fears about vaccination.

articles.title_orig: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.title_zh: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.content_orig:
A Cornell University student gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe in 2024 but expressed dismay over how the authorities handled the case.
The student, who spoke to NBC News on Sunday on condition of anonymity over concerns about repercussions, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus about 24 to 48 hours after the incident. Doe, who filed a lawsuit last month, claimed she was plied with alcohol and ketamine and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house the night of Oct. 19-20.
The student recalled rumors that Doe was planning to have a threesome but that it had “gone off the rails,” and she remembers being “really horrified by it.”
“From that night, I think, we just kind of started, like, hearing more,” the student said.
Talk of the alleged sexual assault became widespread on campus after the school issued a crime safety alert about a report of a sexual assault at a fraternity.
“The thing I think we all feel, like, betrayed in regards to is that, like, it wasn’t handled,” she said. “When we got the police report, I think we all assumed it was being, you know, it would be, like, handled properly, yeah, and it was, like, in good hands.”
The student, who discussed details corroborated by documents reviewed by NBC News, said she and a friend initially gave a tip to authorities after the crime alert was issued. Police later called her and asked her to come in and speak with them days after Doe reported the incident to Cornell police on Nov. 8.
The student said she decided to go to police after she saw screenshots of a Chi Phi group message on Snapchat and because “it felt like the right thing to do if we could help this girl.” Doe’s lawsuit included a screenshot of a Chi Phi Snapchat group message that said there was “free p----” in a room in the frat house where Doe was the night she alleges she was assaulted.
“That was, like, when I kind of internally made the decision. OK, like, I’m taking this all in, and then I’m going to the police tomorrow,” the student said.
She recalled sitting with one or two officers for about half an hour during her interview with police.
“They seemed fairly competent. It seemed like a normal interview process to me,” she said.
She said she walked them through everything she knew, including that fraternity members were messaging about the events of that evening with Doe and about potential witnesses. She also gave police secondhand information about drug use at Chi Phi and said she is familiar with the frat house and believed she knew where ketamine was alleged to be kept.
“I guess I assumed that, like, I wasn’t enough,” the student said.
Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday on the student’s account to police. In a video statement Saturday, President Michael I. Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” and said they raise questions about the investigations that were conducted. He said he welcomes an independent review of how the university handled the matter, which will be conducted by an outside law firm.
Police records obtained by NBC News showed that Cornell police spoke to multiple witnesses and fielded anonymous tips about the allegations of a gang rape at the fraternity house — but that the information was not referred to the local prosecutor for review in his deciding whether to bring charges.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NBC News on Friday that the interviews that were flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.” He did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.
Van Houten ultimately determined the allegations did not warrant charges because of a lack of criminality.
Doe’s suit has sparked uproar and criticism of Cornell and Van Houten’s handling of her allegations. Van Houten has since agreed to reopen his inquiry into Doe’s allegations, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the matter.
The student who spoke with campus police criticized how the department handled the matter. While students believed there was an active investigation into Doe’s claims, people continued going to Chi Phi, including the room at the center of the allegations.
Within Greek life at Cornell, “rumors spread fast,” the student said, and even if you did not know Doe or the men, “you knew someone who did.”
Doe’s lawsuit named Cornell, Chi Phi and the seven fraternity brothers among the defendants. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.
Cornell said in a statement on Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions ” from the university.
According to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation, two of the fraternity members were expelled, and another two were suspected. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and “reflection papers.”
Attorneys for two of the seven men have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the five other men.
Chi Phi’s national fraternity condemned sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in a statement Wednesday. It said that the fraternity members Doe named were kicked out of the organization and that the national fraternity permanently expelled the chapter.
“At every level of Chi Phi, we will take steps like these whenever they are needed to protect the integrity of our fraternity and the safety of our communities,” said Trey Robb, the national fraternity’s interim executive director.
Some of the men faced backlash as talk spread on campus.
Two of the Chi Phi brothers named in the suit were kicked out of their rugby club after the allegations came to light, a former teammate told NBC News.
“We kicked [them] off the team immediately before the school expelled them,” said the teammate, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.
The teammate said he has participated in discussions among a group of current and former rugby players about responding publicly to Doe’s lawsuit.
“As a team, it was important for us to support this victim,” he said. “We are extremely, extremely distraught.”
Cornell Rugby said in a statement that it was “deeply disturbed” by the allegations and that its thoughts were with Doe.
“Players who were known to be connected with the alleged events were permanently removed from the team and alumni network as soon as their affiliation with the incident was established,” it said.
No current members of the team have been affiliated with Chi Phi, the statement said.
As news of the allegations spread, some discussions were supportive of Doe, but others shamed her in conversations, a former member of Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta, told NBC News.
“Some people were sympathizing with Jane Doe, but also, people didn’t know details,” said the former member, who has graduated and requested anonymity out of a concern for privacy.
Another student and former member of Tri Delta told NBC News that she recalled learning about the incident through rumors and described the student body as “really pissed off about it.”
That student said that she was at the same sorority-hosted event the evening of Oct. 19 that Doe attended and which was referred to in her lawsuit but that Doe disappeared during the evening.
A few days later, the student said, Doe said people were spreading rumors about her and she was not sure what to make of it, “and it just seemed like everybody was very confused at the moment.”

articles.title_orig: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.title_zh: How Congo’s Ebola Epidemic Got So Bad So Quickly
articles.content_orig:
Bunia, Congo — Congo's Ebola outbreak has now recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday. They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history .
More than 2,000 patients have recovered from the disease, the Reuters news agency notes.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15 , caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine .
Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak, to demand payment for owed wages. They were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on several strikes since the start of the outbreak to demand payment, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived late Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
"The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.
The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said in its latest news conference that the number of confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hotspots.
A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.
The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in the eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward and he died at a hospital of his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach but those efforts are battling beliefs by some residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

articles.title_orig: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
articles.title_zh: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark
articles.content_orig:
As trawlers compete with Greenland sharks for halibut and cod, conservationists and fishers clash over what to do about misunderstood species
‘W hen I accidentally catch a shark, I bring it to my dogs,” Henrik Jensen, a 27-year-old from Greenland’s west coast, says casually. “I don’t let it back down because [the sharks] bully me and cut my lines.”
Jensen has fished for halibut in Ilulissat, Greenland’s third largest town, for a decade. He works an hour north of the town’s main iceberg-laden fishery, which sustains the livelihood of nearly 400 fishers. There, the halibut are bigger and more plentiful, but so are the Greenland sharks.
“This year I’ve lost around 6,000 hooks in total. Sometimes we lose 30,000 Danish krone [£3,440] a day,” says Jensen.
The Greenland shark is one of the least understood species on the planet. As well as being the world’s slowest shark, it is the second-largest carnivorous species, after the white shark, according to the Shark Trust . Reaching about six to seven metres in length, they can live for more than 400 years. For a long time they were thought to be completely blind, although scientists have recently discovered this may not be true .
The sharks inhabit a vast range across the deep and cold waters of the north and west Atlantic, but their attempts to feed on the northern fisheries’ main catch – Greenland halibut and Atlantic cod – often see them tangled in gear and brought in as bycatch.
This acrimonious coexistence has been documented ever since targeted fishing for the sharks’ liver oil ceased in the 1960s, but it came to a head earlier this year. The Avannaata municipality, of which Ilulissat is the administrative seat, approved a controversial plan to cull 1,000 sharks, offering 300 krone for every heart of a Greenland shark.
Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of the municipality, says: “We need to safeguard the income of fishermen and the catch so that we can continue to eat the foods that we have relied on for generations.”
For many fishing inshore, working in small teams on dinghies, it brought a longstanding issue to a head. Timotheus Petersen, chair of the fishing association in Kullorsuaq, says: “Our longlines are expensive – one costs 1,599 krone. When the sharks cut our lines, we cannot finish fishing. We have to spend more money and buy new gear.”
The plan was eventually dropped after the government questioned its legality, but the prospect of a future cull remains.
In its decision to approve the cull, Avannaata council cited a similar scheme from the early 2000s in the former Aasiaat municipality, where a bounty of 200 krone was offered. According to a 2007 report from the Danish Technical University, another scheme between 1986 and 2001 in the former Uummannaq municipality brought in 19,697 hearts.
But the marine conservation group Oceans North Kalaallit Nunaat (ONKN) argues that culls do not resolve the issue, highlighting the migratory nature of the species, which can swim up to 1,200 miles (2,000km) a year. “Sharks removed in north-west Greenland would quickly be replaced by individuals arriving from other regions,” ONKN warned .
Many fishers also do not consider 300 krone worth the effort of hauling a shark onboard. “It’s difficult to catch them,” Jensen says. “You need bigger hooks and chains for the lines, so I don’t think anyone wants to try.”
But the debate around a possible cull is alarming conservationists. “If somebody says, ‘I’m going to cull a couple of thousand Greenland sharks’, that’s a disaster in my opinion,” says Prof Nick Dulvy, a marine conservationist at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia.
The Greenland shark is believed to become sexually mature at 150, which means the species replaces itself extremely slowly and will not rebound from a cull quickly. It is still recovering from targeted fishing throughout the 19th and mid-20th centuries, when, at its peak in 1948, 58,000 were landed .
“They are probably – biologically – the most sensitive species in the ocean to overfishing,” Dulvy says. Globally, it is estimated that 3,500 sharks are caught every year as bycatch and the population remains in decline.
Greenland’s fishing community highlight their longstanding problem with the sharks, but do not say why it has suddenly escalated. Jenseeraq Poulsen, the director of ONKN, suggests it is due to mounting pressures within a fishing industry that accounts for about 25% of Greenland’s GDP .
“If every Greenland shark in Baffin Bay vanished tomorrow, the inshore fishery in Avannaata would still face too many boats working a quota under pressure, rising costs and no alternative employment,” he says. “When margins are narrow, a longstanding nuisance becomes intolerable.”
Even though the price of halibut continues to rise, according to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the average size of the fish is decreasing annually. While Jensen maintains he can still make a good living from fishing, he describes putting fewer hooks out and bringing in fewer fish, suggesting this is due to overfishing by offshore trawlers.
For some of those fishing these waters, however, the shark is not the leading cause of losing gear. “There are more and more ‘ghost lines’ and they are too heavy to pull up by the machine we use,” Jensen says. Ghost lines are discarded or lost gear that can get entangled with new lines, breaking equipment and trapping marine life.
Halibut Greenland, a cooperatively owned fish-processing company in Ilulissat, provides funds to clean up ghost gear in the area, which ONKN views as more effective than a shark cull. Poulsen also proposes a gear-loss compensation scheme, as well as funded trials of acoustic shark deterrents.
Rebekka Nygård Bak, an adviser to Greenland’s Ministry of Fisheries, Hunting, Agriculture and Self Sufficiency, suggests new bycatch-friendly equipment regulations could be a solution. She says a campaign for better bycatch reporting will also be key to any next steps.
For Poulsen, the sharks and those fishing these waters are two components of the same ecosystem, facing growing pressures in changing seas. “The shark is the visible, tangible version of a problem whose real drivers are structural,” he says.

Russia facing a growing threat from bears A combination of rising bear numbers and shrinking natural food sources in the forests has led to an unprecedented wave of dangerous encounters in Russia this past summer between bears and people, including several human fatalities. Russia’s bear population has more than doubled to over 300,000 in about three decades, leading authorities to urgently seek new authority to curtail the bear surge, according to the independent news outlet Meduza. – Fred Weir
China supercharges its goal for electric and hybrid cars China has unveiled a bold target for electric and hybrid vehicles – aiming for the vehicles to make up 70% of new passenger vehicle sales by 2030. Such sales are already at 59% for the first eight months of this year. But commercial vehicles are lagging behind, in part because of the lack of charging and refueling networks on long-haul truck routes. The government’s five-year blueprint calls for 40% of new commercial vehicles to be electric or hybrid by 2030, up from 34% now. It also sets stricter targets for fuel efficiency and promotes automated driving, according to the Caixin Global financial news outlet. – Ann Scott Tyson
“We want the police to know that workers are not alone.” That’s what a member of a neighborhood patrol in Buenos Aires told the newspaper El País, describing the rationale for monitoring police operations against street vendors and immigrants. Under Argentina’s President Javier Milei, immigration enforcement has become more visible on the streets. In the capital, a group of neighbors has formed to document arrests of migrants and to protect them from alleged abuse by police. The group was inspired by reports of neighborhood organizing in the United States amid Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations.  – Whitney Eulich
“The illusion of illusions” That’s the title of a research paper by Oxford mathematician Alain Goriely challenging the long-standing theory of optical corrections. The myth goes back 2,000 years and holds that the Parthenon, which sits on the Acropolis overlooking Athens, was intentionally constructed with curves to correct various visual illusions and thus appear straight to the human eye. But the theory “does not withstand close examination,” Professor Goriely writes in the Royal Society Open Science journal after conducting mathematical modeling. “The proposed illusions are either unsupported by evidence or too small to have a perceptible effect under typical viewing conditions.” – Matthew Bell

articles.title_orig: RetroGameCon draws gamers, cosplayers from around the world to Syracuse
articles.title_zh: RetroGameCon draws gamers, cosplayers from around the world to Syracuse
articles.content_orig:
Get the latest Syracuse news delivered right to your inbox. Subscribe to our newsletter here .
In the halls of Syracuse’s Oncenter Convention Center, people were greeted by cosplayers wearing detailed handmade designs, like full-body cardboard costumes of Freddy Fazbear from “ Five Nights at Freddy’s ” and 3D-printed wands to mimic Madoka Kaname from “ Madoka Magica .”
These were just two of the characters that retro game enthusiasts dressed as for the 13th annual RetroGameCon , which took place from Friday to Sunday. The convention center’s two floors were lined with retro video game consoles, welcoming crowds to share their interests throughout the weekend.
“Everyone was really welcoming and friendly,” attendee Sonny Schiano said. “I was really expecting it to be more niche, specifically retro games, but I was really happy to find out that there’s so many different communities. Everyone’s been really cool so far.”
Schiano, a junior at Duke University, flew from North Carolina for a weekend of retro video games. He heard about the event from one of his high school teachers and decided to meet up with friends from other schools at the convention this past weekend.
Hobbyists from all fandoms, like “ Resident Evil ” and “ One Piece ,” came together to play games, cosplay and meet celebrity guest actors, despite the loyalties they may have to different games and franchises. Celebrities like Jennifer Hale , who previously held the Guinness World Record for the most prolific female video game voice actor, and performance actor Nick Apostolides , who played Leon Kennedy in the video game series “Resident Evil,” were among the guests who visited the convention.
Started in 2013 by Ed Forth, RetroGameCon is the largest pop culture event in Syracuse and upstate New York, bringing more than 10,000 attendees throughout the three-day convention, event coordinator Nathan Grant said.
“We get a lot of compliments from local businesses that say that was our busiest weekend in a long time because so many people are coming to travel here now,” Grant said. “It’s not just locals that attend that we see a lift in the area economically.”
When walking into the convention, attendees were greeted by a community of people wearing intricate cosplay designs and carrying detailed props into the main space with over 200 vendors, including illustrator and manga artist Len Nicholas . Nicholas is a professional artist who went viral for his cute sketches of “ Pokemon ” in different scenarios, such as Pikachu with a machine gun and hyperrealistic versions of animated characters, such as Bender from “ Futurama .”
Tattoo buffs admire artistry behind ink, stencils at Villain Arts Festival
From Sept. 18 to 20, the Villain Arts Tattoo Festival held its first annual Syracuse convention, bringing tattooists of all styles and aesthetics.
“Art, in my opinion, is connection. So you really want to connect with the people that come to your booth,” Nicholas said. “They’re nice enough to take an interest in something you’ve created. I like to take an interest and reciprocate as well.”
For the past two years, Nicholas has attended the convention from Elmira, New York, not only to bond with his daughter, but to use the convention as a business opportunity to connect and sell his art. Since appearing at the convention, Len has expanded his business ventures to selling art at other local conventions.
“It actually turned into something that was kind of lucrative,” Nicholas said. “I’m a professional artist, and it’s been a nice little income addition, especially with the advent of AI kind of cutting into our business.”
Other vendors were selling video games, console parts, card trading, merchandise and more. Surrounding the vendor booths were vintage gaming consoles, like Macintosh computers and “ Tetris ,” bringing back video games from decades ago.
The lower level of the convention featured different sections dedicated to card games, panels, live-action role-play jousting tournaments, an extensive food court and cosplay contests. During the contests,people of all ages were applauded for their original clothing designs showcasing their favorite fictional characters like Princess Peach and Lisa from “ Death Note .”
The center was bustling with fans from across the world, taking in the sights, buying merchandise, playing games and enjoying time with their respective communities —  something Grant loves most about the convention.
“The more this thing grows, the more people that want to help come together and put it on grows as well,” Grant said.
For Grant, RetroGameCon is only “a name.” The event not only focuses on retro gaming, but also preserves the culture and nostalgia of classic video games while bringing different fandoms together under one roof, Grant said.
A fan of the video game “ Dead by Daylight ” and third-year attendee Laura Pellegrino admires how the convention gives people a place to talk about their love for a wide variety of fandoms.
“I really like seeing the new types of fandom,” Pellegrino said. “Something I might not have dipped my toes into and getting to interact with those people.”
Attendees browse different designs of “Dungeons & Dragons” dice at RetroGameCon. The three-day convention also featured cosplayers dressed as video game characters and celebrity guests. Daniel Carson | Contributing Photographer
Many attendees don’t solely go for a specific hobby. People generally have multiple pop culture interests that overlap, like Schiano, who enjoys “ Jojo’s Bizarre Adventure ” and “ Team Fortress 2 .” Schiano initially worried that the convention would exclusively focus on retro games, but was happy to find modern titles represented as well, with vendors selling games like Mario Kart World or Persona 5 Royal .
“There’s a variety, and I think that’s really cool,” Schiano said. “It’s like when we first heard RetroGameCon, like I thought it was just kind of like exclusively for that. But there’s a lot of modern games and pop culture too.”
Not only does the convention help people find a community and share interests, but the organization also has a charitable aspect that supports local businesses and hospitals.
A few years after the convention began, organizers introduced charity raffles and auctions for Extra Life, a program supporting Children’s Miracle Network Hospitals and Upstate University Golisano Children’s Hospital in Syracuse, Grant said.
For Grant and the rest of the organization, the convention is about more than giving attendees a place to play games and buy merchandise. It’s an opportunity for people with shared interests to meet one another and form lasting connections.
“Friendships are made here,” Grant said. “You get to see that firsthand, not just through the attendees, but through the people putting it on. We’re really building a solid community.”

articles.title_orig: Orion browser for Linux axed months after beta launch
articles.title_zh: Orion browser for Linux axed months after beta launch
articles.content_orig:
Kagi has announced that it is ending the development of the Orion web browser for Linux.
The native GTK port of Orion for Linux was announced in 2025 and a public beta launched earlier this year. The goal was feature parity with the macOS build. Recent beta releases edged closer to realising it but, alas, fell short – and that’s where things will stay.
Kagi says it plans to open source the Orion for Linux codebase, as well its WIP port of Orion for Windows. This could enable the FOSS community the opportunity to step up and “carry them forward”– not that developing an independent web browser will be easy.
“Building a cross-platform browser is something usually done by companies backed by venture capital or by large open-source communities” , it said in a statement, adding that it is neither, employing just a handful of developers funded by users of its paid search engine.
It could’ve made life easier had if it had done what most modern browsers do and build on Chromium. Kagi said it felt the web “needs more than one engine” and, ideally, more than one company able to shape what the web looks like.
I find Orion on macOS to be a genuinely solid browser and I had been hopeful that, despite the herculean task, the Kagi team had the skills and ideas to pull it off – however slow going it was.
Orion wasn’t open-source from the get-go, which, for some in the FOSS community, had soured any enthusiasm towards it. Bittersweet news that, now, it is.
Kagi’s business model (i.e., funded by users and thus building only for them) was would’ve meant a browser developed for users, without any need to stuff the UI with attention hijacking gimmicks or integrate partner deals to bump revenue.
And, in a sense, it’s that business model pulling Kagi’s focus back to Orion for macOS and iOS: it’s where its users are.
Hopefully, the decision to open-source where they got to can help drive Orion forward in some guise, or at least have its parts picked over to benefit other independent web browser efforts.
Development on Orion for macOS and iOS is unaffected by this change, but the Linux beta will see no further update. If you installed it, you can keep using it, though Kagi says it doesn’t recommend using it as a daily driver as as security issues will remain unpatched.
Kagi has said it will share more details about the codebase open-sourcing in the coming month.

articles.title_zh: New World screwworm cases climb to 53; new case confirmed in Brewster County dog
articles.content_orig:
Houston Matters is live! Join the conversation: Email | Call/Text | Watch | Listen
Last updated: Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026 7:00 p.m
There have now been 53 confirmed New World screwworm animal cases in the United States since June, including 51 in Texas and two in New Mexico.
The latest case was confirmed Oct. 2 in a dog in Brewster County, Texas. It is one of three animal cases currently considered active.
The other active cases are goats in Crockett County, Texas, confirmed Sept. 26, and a horse in Grant County, New Mexico, confirmed Sept. 17.
A horse in Presidio County, Texas, confirmed Sept. 9 and previously listed as active, is now considered inactive.
Officials have also recorded one wild screwworm fly detection during the current U.S. outbreak. The fly was found in a surveillance trap in Brewster County on Sept. 25. Fly trap detections are tracked separately and are not included in the 53 animal cases.
Of the 53 animal cases recorded since the first U.S. case was confirmed June 3, 52 have involved domestic animals. No cases have been confirmed in wildlife or feral animals.
Federal officials have said the parasite’s northward spread has slowed, though the threat remains.
The USDA says it has released more than 1 billion sterile flies in Texas since February and is aiming to increase production to 500 million flies a week by next summer.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins has said officials are making progress in containing the outbreak but have warned that the threat has not passed, particularly in Arizona and New Mexico.
Despite its name, the New World screwworm isn’t a worm. It is the larval stage of the fly (Cochliomyia hominivorax), a parasite that feeds on the living tissue of warm-blooded animals.
Infestations begin when an adult female screwworm fly lays eggs in an open wound or natural body opening. Within hours, the eggs hatch and the larvae begin feeding on living tissue, unlike common maggots, which feed on dead or decaying tissue.
As the larvae burrow deeper into tissue, wounds become larger and often infected. Without treatment, infestations can be fatal.
The screwworm primarily threatens livestock and wildlife, making it a major concern for Texas ranchers and animal health officials.
Human infestations are rare. Most occur when untreated wounds are exposed in areas where the fly is circulating. The current outbreak primarily affects livestock, wildlife and pets.
According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, New World screwworm is not considered a food safety threat. The parasite feeds on living tissue in open wounds — not meat intended for consumers — and animal health and inspection systems are designed to keep infested animals out of the food supply.
Early detection is critical. Animals infected with screwworm may show:
Veterinarians recommend inspecting animals regularly after injuries, surgical procedures, branding or any condition that creates an open wound.
Texas has one of the largest livestock industries in the United States, along with extensive ranchland and abundant wildlife populations, particularly white-tailed deer. That combination makes the state especially vulnerable if screwworm becomes reestablished.
A widespread outbreak could lead to:
The Texas Animal Health Commission and the U.S. Department of Agriculture have expanded surveillance, increased monitoring of animal movement and encouraged rapid reporting of suspected infestations.
The United States eliminated screwworm using one of the most successful pest control programs in history: the sterile insect technique.
Scientists bred and released millions of sterile male flies. Because female screwworm flies typically mate only once, breeding with a sterile male produces no offspring, gradually collapsing the wild population.
That strategy eradicated screwworm from the United States and much of North America. However, the parasite remains present in parts of Central and South America, meaning the risk of reintroduction never fully disappears.
For most Texans, there is no reason to change their daily activities. The greatest risk remains to livestock, pets and wildlife.
Hunters should also inspect harvested game for unusual wounds or signs of infestation and report suspected cases to wildlife officials.
If you suspect an infestation, contact your veterinarian immediately before transporting the animal.
For the latest information and guidance, visit:
The illegal movement of animals — particularly horses — could thwart the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s effort to stop the spread of the parasite.
Texas A&M AgriLife livestock entomologist Sonja Swiger discusses the risks New World screwworm poses to pets, people and livestock, addresses concerns about the food supply and explains why reporting infestations is critical.
Wildlife experts warn that deer may be especially vulnerable because there is no proven way to treat them in the wild.
The New World screwworm has crossed into Texas from Mexico, threatening livestock, wildlife and pets. Human infections are rare, but officials warn the parasite’s spread poses a growing challenge for communities across South Texas.
As the U.S. confronts the return of New World screwworm, researchers at the newly opened Knipling-Bushland U.S. Livestock Insects Research Laboratory in Kerrville are building on the work that helped eradicate the pest decades ago.
The Texas agriculture commissioner supports the move by the federal agency.

Windows powers how people around the world work, learn, create, and connect every day. Today, we’re announcing the availability of the Windows 11 2026 Update, also known as Windows 11, version 26H2. Built on the same servicing foundation as recent Windows 11 releases, version 26H2 delivers the latest Windows innovations with a streamlined update experience designed to minimize disruption and help you stay secure, productive, and up to date.
As organizations and individuals continue to expect faster deployments and less downtime, Windows 11, version 26H2 takes advantage of the same modern servicing technologies that have simplified recent feature updates. For many eligible devices, moving to version 26H2 is as simple as installing a small enablement package, allowing people to start using this new release with minimal download size, quick installation, and a single restart.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is delivered as an enablement package for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
An enablement package is a lightweight update that activates new features already included in the operating system through previous monthly servicing updates. Because versions 26H2, 25H2, and 24H2 share a common servicing branch and underlying codebase, many of the components required for version 26H2 are already present on devices before the feature update becomes available.
This approach enables a significantly faster update experience compared to a traditional operating system upgrade. For eligible devices, installation is similar to a monthly update, requiring only a small download and a quick restart to transition to Windows 11, version 26H2.
As with every Windows release, version 26H2 includes the latest quality, reliability, and security improvements designed to help protect people and organizations while delivering a dependable Windows experience.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is now available for eligible devices running Windows 11, versions 25H2 and 24H2.
To be among the first to receive the update, go to Settings > Windows Update and turn on Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available . Once your device is eligible, you’ll see the option to download and install Windows 11, version 26H2.
As always, we take a measured and data-driven approach to broad availability and will be releasing version 26H2 using a controlled feature rollout. During rollout, we might place safeguard holds on devices where we detect a known compatibility issue that could impact the update experience. We will continue expanding availability over time and provide updates through the Windows release health hub.
Windows 11, version 26H2 is available now through the tools organizations use to manage Windows updates, including Windows Autopatch and the Microsoft 365 admin center [i] .
Existing management tools, update rings, policies, and deployment practices can continue to be used. We recommend that commercial and education customers begin targeted deployments to validate applications, devices, and business-critical workflows before expanding deployment more broadly throughout their organizations.
Windows 11, version 26H2 continues the annual Windows feature update cadence, with a new Windows 11 feature update released during the second half of the calendar year. As with previous annual releases, installing version 26H2 resets the support lifecycle for supported editions of Windows 11. That means 24 months of support for Home and Pro editions and 36 months of support for Enterprise and Education editions.
Select features and enhancements initially released as disabled by default in version 25H2 will be enabled by default in version 26H2. You can find more information on these features, plus guidance to help with planning and deployment, in the Windows IT Pro Blog .
We recommend updating eligible devices to Windows 11, version 26H2 to take advantage of the latest Windows innovations, quality improvements, and security enhancements.
We’ll continue to closely monitor the rollout and share information about known issues, safeguards, and rollout progress through the Windows release health hub and official Windows communications channels.
Thank you for your feedback and partnership as we continue to improve Windows for people and organizations around the world. We love to hear about your experience, so please keep your comments and suggestions coming in via Feedback Hub.
[i] Downloads in the Microsoft 365 admin center and similar channels may be delayed.

articles.title_orig: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
articles.title_zh: Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma Beddington
articles.content_orig:
Their careers are peaking, they’re rich in money and time – and young people think they’re cool. But maybe it’s not as simple as that
‘S top sleeping on gen X.” I heard this on TikTok recently. I misinterpreted it, with a guilty start, as: “Stop sleeping, gen X,” because I am 51 (peak X), so always tired; while not sleeping at the time, I may have been resting my eyes. In fact, Joel Marlinarson, a marketing guru , was suggesting my generation have become a powerful, if underrated, force online.
Aged between 46 and 61, gen Xers with proper jobs are peaking, career-wise (although it’s a different story for those out of work, as a report last month on the struggles of over-50s jobseekers made plain). We’re more likely to own homes than the following generations ; we’re emerging from the trenches of childrearing and, the argument goes, ready to indulge in some me-time. “If gen X were a country, it would be the world’s second-largest consumer market,” the World Economic Forum reported last year , with gen X women in particular influencing 70% to 80% of all consumer spending.
That makes us great customers – witness the tidal wave of menopause-washed wellness guff (Which? reported last month that many pricey supplements were no better than a cheap multivitamin ) and beauty brands for people suddenly horrified by their necks . But does it give us content-creating clout? We’re supposed to be (or at least meme lore presents us as ) the forgotten generation, low-key, countercultural slackers on the sidelines in the grudge match between millennials and boomers; aspiration and self-promotion aren’t really part of our brand.
Sure, kids are scrambling for Oasis tickets and rediscovering zines ; US Vogue called us “the cool ones” and the New York Times went further with “the greatest generation”. I get the argument that it’s our time to shine. But real gen Xers have a lot on their plate and it doesn’t necessarily lend itself to fun, aspirational content.
Being peak career means peak responsibility: our parents are faltering (I’m writing this as my mother-in-law is moving into sheltered accommodation) and our kids are facing awful geopolitical and economic prospects that undermine their mental health and chances of independence. We’re falling apart physically: for women, the sorting hat of perimenopause doles out a set of grim symptoms, while men are wondering what will fell them next – heart, stomach, back or knees? Who wants to hear about that? And who can be arsed to make perky TikToks?
I’ll tell you who: Kathryn Turner . I was introduced to Turner, M&S Food’s director of product development, by Marlinarson, for whom she is evidence that over-50s employees are “ the next biggest influencers ”. Turner, a cheery woman in smart trousers who exudes quiet competence, has worked for M&S since 1995. She launched her account in May, but her TikToks already garner up to 2m views and her nearly 250,000 fans are devoted: “Would follow that woman into war,” commented one . “Why did we give Andy Burnham the job over her,” asked another . “ I love you Kathryn turner [sic],” wrote an account claiming to be the Heartstopper actor Joe Locke . I love her, too: Turner’s calm sunniness, as she talks viewers through innovations in the picky bits space, is a balm in a fractious world.
Turner isn’t Kate Moss, Miranda July or any of the other impossibly glamorous gen X figureheads – she seems like a normal, middle-aged woman who knows her stuff and does it well. I love that she’s popping up on TikTok and I get it – I’m projecting, but I bet Turner’s great in a crisis, her desk drawer and handbag well stocked with protein-rich treats, blister plasters and ibuprofen.
Maybe this is our online USP. Could watching grownups quietly bossing their busy, complex lives be the next ASMR? Because, mostly, gen X aren’t the “cool ones”: they’re the knackered ones, dealing with life, death, work and frozen shoulders. I don’t know any Mosses or Chloë Sevignys, but I know lots of Turners and I, too, would follow them into war, or at least get a dopamine hit from watching them be extremely competent in short-form videos. No one would want to watch me staring at a screen then breaking to fold some pants, obviously, but I’d love to see more of my capable peers ditch the self-deprecation (very gen X) and shine online.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

An appeal for wars to end and for peace to be built. The Pope renewed this appeal following the recitation of the Angelus prayer he led from the window of the Apostolic Palace. As he did during his recent visit to Lourdes, France, he again urged everyone to pray the Rosary for peace and unity in the world, standing in solidarity with children who have already begun doing so through the initiative of the Aid to the Church in Need Foundation, âOne Million Children Praying the Holy Rosary.â
âI wholeheartedly thank all the boys and girls who are joining in this prayer in so many parts of the world.  Let us all follow their example, invoking the intercession of the Virgin Mary so that peoples may be freed from the scourge of war.  In particular, let us pray for the Holy Land and for the innocent victims of violence.â
The campaign began at the start of October with the Pope in the Vatican Gardens and will continue until October 7, the Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary. This allows dioceses, parishes, schools, communities, and families on different continents to choose the day that is most suitable for dedicating to this particular intention.
Pope Leo then announced that, on the occasion of the tenth anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, Pope Francisâs post-synodal apostolic exhortation, a week-long gathering will begin next Wednesday, October 7.
It will be held in his presence in the Paul VI Hall, with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Episcopal Conferences, to take stock of the situation of families today. The gathering will include testimonies from bishops and married couples from the five continents.
It will be an opportunity to listen to the voice of the Church at a time of profound change and to find ways to renew and strengthen the choice of marriage, which in various contexts has experienced dramatic declines over the decades. The Pontiff described it this way:
âIt will be a time of synodal discernment for identifying the steps to be taken in order to proclaim the Gospel today among families and the younger generations.  I entrust this task to your prayers and, above all, the families who, with Godâs help, are a sign of hope and an inestimable treasure for the Church and for society.â
The Pope then once again held up Saint Francis as a model, as he had done during the catechesis, on the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis. He expressed his happiness at the many commemorative initiatives, particularly those held in Assisi with the participation of Italyâs highest state authorities. He also offered a special greeting:
âI also greet the amateur radio operators of Assisi and Foligno who spread Saint Francisâ message of peace.â
